name: Surendra Maharjan
headline: PhD Researcher
about: I'm a PhD researcher focused on hydroclimate extremes, water resources, and machine learning. My work combines remote sensing, reanalysis/climate datasets, and statistical learning to understand and predict droughts, floods, and compound events.
I'm especially interested in building reproducible, scalable workflows in Python/R and translating scientific results into practical tools for risk assessment and decision support.

highlights.statLabel: of normal annual flow lost in multi-year droughts
highlights.title: Drought–flood whiplash will hit the least resilient US counties hardest
highlights.text: Normalized streamflow from USGS records and downscaled projections shows sharp regional disparities. Counties with the deepest droughts also face the highest annual losses and lowest resilience (FEMA National Risk Index).
highlights.imageAlt: Maps of projected drought deficits and wet surpluses across the US under RCP 4.5 and 8.5

highlights.statLabel: decline in peak snowpack under high emissions
highlights.title: Physics-informed deep learning forecasts snowpack loss
highlights.text: A physics-informed LSTM beat both SWAT and a plain LSTM. Projections show peak discharge down about 33% and snowmelt runoff arriving 10–19 days earlier, squeezing summer water for ecosystems.
highlights.imageAlt: Map of the Upper West Walker River watershed in California, with elevation and monitoring sites

highlights.statLabel: vapor pressure deficit limit for crop water-use efficiency
highlights.title: Machine learning maps Egypt’s crops and their water use
highlights.text: Support vector machines mapped rice, wheat and clover across the Nile Valley and Delta. Above a VPD of 3.5 kPa, water-use efficiency stops responding, and CMIP6 projects more such months.
highlights.imageAlt: Crop maps of rice, wheat and clover along the Nile Valley and Delta, Egypt

highlights.statLabel: of Western US stations critically dry in 2021
highlights.title: Hydrological extremes are escalating in the Western US
highlights.text: A new water-year index shows more extremes and whiplash since 2015 in every basin; over 54% of stations were extremely wet in 2023. Frontline communities bear disproportionate drought impacts.
highlights.imageAlt: Maps of extreme wet and dry water years across Western US basins

highlights.title: Pacific climate patterns drive whiplash events
highlights.text: Wet–dry whiplash is strongly linked to the Western Pacific and East Pacific/North Pacific oscillations, with ENSO and the Madden–Julian Oscillation adding to Pacific Southwest wet spells.
highlights.imageAlt: Maps of projected precipitation variability across the Western US

highlights.statLabel: monsoon impacts projected with 5 CMIP6 models
highlights.title: A longer monsoon brings bigger floods to a Himalayan basin
highlights.text: SWAT projections show an extended rainy season, higher annual discharge and more extreme flows, while drier pre-monsoon spells raise wildfire and landslide risk.
highlights.imageAlt: Graphical abstract: changing monsoon, streamflow and hazards in the Indrawati River Basin, Nepal
